testcases.scenario: Demonstrates how coverpoints can monitor computed expressions rather than just raw signals, including comparisons, arithmetic operations, and bit extractions. This example shows practical expression coverage patterns like overflow detection, equality checks, and modulo operations on ALU operands.

testcases.title: Generic Coverage Groups
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates parameterized and generic covergroups in SystemVerilog using reference arguments, sample-time arguments, and conditional sampling (iff) to create reusable coverage components that can monitor multiple signals with similar coverage goals.

testcases.title: Coverage Bins
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates automatic bin creation in SystemVerilog functional coverage, showing how coverpoints automatically partition variable ranges into bins and how auto_bin_max controls bin granularity. Illustrates both implicit bin generation and explicit bin array syntax for different coverage strategies.

testcases.title: Explicit Bin Creation
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates explicit bin creation in SystemVerilog coverage to partition the input space into meaningful ranges and values. This example shows single-value bins, range bins, multi-value bins, and array-generated bins for classifying memory controller commands, addresses, burst lengths, and priority levels.

testcases.title: Transition Bins
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates state transition coverage using SystemVerilog covergroups with transition bins (=>) to track FSM state sequences. Shows single transitions (A => B), multi-step sequences (A => B => C), and constraint-driven valid state paths for protocol verification.

testcases.title: Wildcard Bins
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates wildcard bins using '?' and 'x' metacharacters in functional coverage to match groups of values with common bit patterns. Wildcard bins enable efficient coverage specification where a single bin definition covers multiple related values, reducing the number of explicit bins needed.

testcases.title: Ignore Bins
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates the use of ignore_bins in SystemVerilog covergroups to exclude specific values from coverage calculation. This example shows how reserved, unused, or don't-care values can be marked as ignored so they don't affect coverage percentages, using command codes, address regions, and priority levels as practical examples.

testcases.title: Illegal Bins
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates the use of illegal_bins in functional coverage to mark values that should never occur in a design, generating runtime errors/warnings when sampled to catch protocol violations and invalid states.

testcases.title: Cross Coverage
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates cross coverage between multiple coverpoints to verify combinations of command types, address ranges, transfer sizes, and priority levels. Shows how cross coverage helps identify corner cases and ensure all interesting value combinations are tested, including constraint interactions like RMW operations avoiding high priority.

testcases.title: Coverage Options
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates key coverage options in SystemVerilog: per_instance for separate instance tracking, weight for coverage importance, goal for target percentages, and at_least for minimum hit requirements. These options enable fine-grained control over coverage calculation and reporting in functional verification.

testcases.title: Coverage Methods
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates SystemVerilog coverage methods for querying and controlling coverage collection, including get_coverage() for type-level metrics, get_inst_coverage() for instance-specific metrics, and start/stop methods to enable/disable sampling. Shows practical usage with multiple covergroup instances and both explicit and auto-sampling techniques.

testcases.title: Cover Property
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates cover properties for tracking sequence and temporal behavior coverage in functional verification. Shows how to define sequences (req-gnt handshake, valid-ready, burst transactions, back-to-back requests) and use cover properties to measure whether specific scenarios are exercised during simulation, complementing value-based covergroups.

testcases.title: Buggy Functional Coverage Exercise1
testcases.scenario: ALU with functional coverage model containing three intentional bugs: covergroup sampling on negedge instead of posedge, overlapping bins for operand_a coverage, and incorrect cross-coverage ignore_bins syntax. Students must identify and fix these coverage construct issues.

testcases.title: Buggy Functional Coverage Exercise2
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates functional coverage issues in a protocol verification module with three distinct bugs: a covergroup that is declared but never instantiated, a coverpoint referencing an incorrect signal name, and a malformed transition bin syntax. Students must identify why coverage data will not be collected and fix the covergroup instantiation and signal references.

testcases.title: Buggy Cover Group Ex1
testcases.scenario: This exercise contains three bugs in a covergroup definition for a simple data register with state tracking: the covergroup is instantiated before proper construction, the sample event is missing the clocking event trigger, and a coverpoint references an undeclared signal name instead of the correct state variable.

testcases.title: Buggy Cover Group Ex2
testcases.scenario: UART transaction coverage exercise where the covergroup uses an incorrect sampling condition (iff(rst)) that gates all coverage collection to only the reset window. After reset de-asserts, no further samples are collected despite heavy stimulus, leaving coverage near 0%.

testcases.title: Buggy Sample Ex1
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates functional coverage sampling issues in SystemVerilog, where a covergroup fails to properly capture design behavior due to incorrect sample() calls, missing event triggers, and lack of reset guards. Students must identify why coverage remains incomplete and fix the sampling mechanism.

testcases.title: Buggy Sample Ex2
testcases.scenario: Sample exercise demonstrating a functional coverage bug where the covergroup sample() method is conditionally gated on the reset signal, preventing coverage collection during normal operation when meaningful stimulus is applied. The DUT memory logic functions correctly, but coverage metrics are never captured.

testcases.title: Buggy Cover Points Ex1
testcases.scenario: GPIO controller with functional coverage that monitors direction, output value, and enable signal. The design demonstrates coverpoint definition but contains an inverted guard condition that prevents proper sampling of the enable signal state.

testcases.title: Buggy Cover Points Ex2
testcases.scenario: Timer module with functional coverage bugs including a coverpoint defined on a wire instead of an internal variable, an invalid bin range with inverted bounds, and incorrect syntax for the auto bin count option. This exercise teaches proper coverage model construction and bin specification.

testcases.title: Buggy Coverpoint Expression Ex1
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates three functional coverage bugs in coverpoint expressions: a syntax error (missing operator in expression), use of blocking assignment instead of comparison operator, and bin ranges that exceed the expression's bit width. Students must identify and fix these errors to properly capture coverage for an adder module.

testcases.title: Buggy Coverpoint Expression Ex2
testcases.scenario: This exercise contains a buggy coverpoint expression that uses bitwise AND (&&) instead of equality comparison (==) in cp_port_match, causing incorrect bin coverage. Students must identify why the logical operation produces wrong results and fix it to properly track source/destination port matching patterns.

testcases.title: Buggy Generic Coverage Groups Ex1
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates a covergroup with explicit sampling that is never invoked, resulting in 0% coverage despite active simulation. The design contains an 8-bit register pair with XOR output and a covergroup parameterized with a sample() function, but the sampling call is missing from the sequential logic block.

testcases.title: Buggy Generic Coverage Groups Ex2
testcases.scenario: A module that captures data from two input channels with valid signals into registered outputs, then multiplexes them. The covergroup uses an explicit 'with function sample(...)' clause that disables automatic sampling, but the design never calls sample() explicitly, leaving coverage at 0% despite exercising the logic.

testcases.title: Buggy Coverage Bins Ex1
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates a functional coverage measurement bug where an iff guard condition on a coverpoint unintentionally excludes the middle bin from being sampled. The coverpoint is defined with three bins (low [0:63], mid [64:191], high [192:255]), but the iff guard only allows sampling when data is outside the [64:191] range, making the 'mid' bin impossible to hit and capping coverage at 67%.

testcases.title: Buggy Coverage Bins Ex2
testcases.scenario: SystemVerilog coverage bins exercise with three deliberate bugs: using array bin syntax on a single-value set, attempting to define a bin with a string literal instead of numeric values, and specifying a reversed range for positive operand values. This exercise teaches proper coverage bin syntax and range specification.

testcases.title: Buggy Explicit Bin Creation Ex1
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates a critical functional coverage bug where explicit bins are created for incorrect command values (4-7) while the actual valid commands (0-3) are marked as ignore_bins, causing coverage collection to fail silently. The testbench drives valid transactions with commands 0-3, but none are counted toward coverage because they're ignored by the coverpoint.

testcases.title: Buggy Explicit Bin Creation Ex2
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates a mismatch between declared coverpoint bins and actual stimulus values. The cp_channel coverpoint declares bins for values {4,5,6,7}, but the testbench only drives channel with values {0,1,2,3}, resulting in 0% coverage for that coverpoint and failing to meet the overall 80% coverage goal.

testcases.title: Buggy Transition Bins Ex1
testcases.scenario: This exercise contains three distinct bugs in transition bin definitions within a covergroup for an FSM state coverage model. Students must identify and fix incorrect transition syntax (comma vs. arrow operator), invalid repetition syntax in transitions, and type mismatches between transition values and the coverpoint range.

testcases.title: Buggy Transition Bins Ex2
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates three distinct bugs in SystemVerilog transition bin syntax: using range operator (..) incorrectly within transition arrows, misusing goto repetition syntax ([->]) in bin definitions, and applying non-consecutive repetition syntax ([=]) without a proper range specification. The exercise highlights the critical distinction between valid bin transition contexts and improper syntax usage.

testcases.title: Buggy Wildcard Bins Ex1
testcases.scenario: Buggy exercise demonstrating multiple wildcard bin definition errors in functional coverage. The covergroup attempts to define wildcard bins for an instruction decoder but contains syntax errors, semantic mismatches between wildcard patterns and variable widths, and inconsistent bin configurations that prevent proper coverage collection.

testcases.title: Buggy Wildcard Bins Ex2
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates wildcard bin mismatches in functional coverage, including overlapping bins in one coverpoint and an incorrectly sized wildcard pattern in another. Students must identify why certain bins never get covered despite seemingly valid sampling.

testcases.title: Buggy Ignore Bins Ex1
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates incorrect usage of ignore_bins in functional coverage, including syntax errors (singular vs. plural keyword), semantic errors (range overlaps that eliminate all valid coverage), and structural errors (placement outside coverpoint blocks). Students must identify and fix three distinct bugs related to coverage exclusion.

testcases.title: Buggy Ignore Bins Ex2
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates incorrect usage of ignore_bins with cross coverage and transitions. It contains three bugs: using && instead of intersect in cross ignore_bins, incorrect transition arrow syntax in ignore_bins, and improper binsof() syntax when referencing coverpoints.

testcases.title: Buggy Illegal Bins Ex1
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates incorrect usage of illegal_bins in functional coverage, including wrong keyword spelling, overlapping range definitions, and incorrect transition syntax. Students must identify and fix three distinct bugs that prevent proper illegal bin specification and coverage measurement.

testcases.title: Buggy Illegal Bins Ex2
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates multiple illegal_bins usage errors in functional coverage: attempting to use illegal_bins within cross coverage (not allowed), using incorrect value syntax, and defining a coverpoint with only illegal_bins and no normal bins.

testcases.title: Buggy Cross Coverage Ex1
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates a covergroup sampling guard condition bug where `iff (rst)` prevents the covergroup from sampling after reset is released. The cross coverage between address and data signals never accumulates because the sampling event only fires while reset is asserted, leaving the cross coverpoint at 0% coverage despite extensive stimulus.

testcases.title: Buggy Cross Coverage Ex2
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates three common cross coverage bugs: using 'bins' instead of 'bins=' for explicit cross bin definitions, referencing a non-existent coverpoint member (cp_dst.port instead of cp_dst.ports), and attempting to create a cross coverage between coverpoints from different covergroups which is not supported in SystemVerilog.

testcases.title: Buggy Coverage Options Ex1
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates functional coverage configuration options in SystemVerilog covergroups, including goal setting, at_least thresholds, and proper use of option keywords. The code contains three bugs: an invalid goal value (200 exceeds max of 100), a misspelled at_least keyword (atleast), and incorrect use of type_option at instance level instead of option.

testcases.title: Buggy Coverage Options Ex2
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates a functional coverage configuration bug where option.at_least = 1000 requires each bin to be hit 1000 times before counting as covered. With only ~80 stimulus cycles in the testbench, typical bins receive far fewer hits, causing get_coverage() to return near 0% even though the design functions correctly.

testcases.title: Buggy Coverage Methods Ex1
testcases.scenario: Functional coverage collection is instantiated but immediately disabled via cg_inst.stop() before any stimulus is applied, causing coverage to remain at 0% despite correct RTL logic and extensive test stimulus. This exercise demonstrates the critical mistake of disabling coverage prematurely.

testcases.title: Buggy Coverage Methods Ex2
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates improper use of SystemVerilog covergroup methods, specifically calling stop() without start(), which disables sampling entirely. Students must identify why coverage collection fails and understand the lifecycle of covergroup sampling control.

testcases.title: Buggy System Tasks Ex1
testcases.scenario: This exercise contains a buggy SystemVerilog coverage system tasks implementation with syntax errors in covergroup sampling calls and incomplete code. Students must identify and fix the missing function arguments and unclosed statements that prevent proper functional coverage collection.

testcases.title: Buggy System Tasks Ex2
testcases.scenario: SystemVerilog coverage system tasks exercise with incomplete code and multiple coverage-related issues. Students must identify bugs in covergroup instantiation, sampling, and coverage database management calls.

testcases.title: Buggy Cover Property Ex1
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates a functional coverage bug where a covergroup transition bin (1 => 1) expects req to remain high for two consecutive clock cycles, but the protocol only asserts req for exactly one cycle, resulting in 0% coverage despite valid handshakes occurring repeatedly.

testcases.title: Buggy Cover Property Ex2
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates three common coverage property bugs: using assert instead of cover for coverage collection, referencing an undeclared signal (htrans instead of hsel) in a property sequence, and assigning duplicate labels to different cover properties. Students must identify and fix these issues to properly collect functional coverage on AHB protocol write and read cycles.

testcases.title: Sv Events
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates SystemVerilog event declaration, triggering with the -> operator, and waiting with the @ operator for inter-process communication. Shows practical patterns including producer-consumer synchronization, event.triggered property usage, and multiple processes coordinating through events.

testcases.title: Nonblocking Events
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates SystemVerilog nonblocking event triggers (->>) and their critical difference from blocking triggers (->). Shows how nonblocking event scheduling in the NBA (Nonblocking Assignment) region prevents race conditions and ensures predictable event synchronization across concurrent processes.

testcases.title: Wait Order In Sv Events
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates SystemVerilog's wait_order() construct for verifying that events occur in a specific sequence. Shows how to detect both correct protocol ordering and out-of-order event violations, essential for protocol verification in digital designs.

testcases.title: Merging Events In Sv
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates SystemVerilog event variables and merging, showing how assigning one event to another creates aliases that point to the same event object. When merged events are triggered, all waiters on any of the merged event handles are awakened simultaneously.

testcases.title: Passing An Event
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates passing SystemVerilog events as constructor arguments and task parameters to enable event-based synchronization between classes. Shows patterns for shared events, broadcast communication, and producer-consumer coordination through event passing.

testcases.title: Sv Semaphores
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates SystemVerilog semaphores for inter-process communication, covering semaphore creation, blocking key acquisition with get(), non-blocking access with try_get(), and key return with put() for mutual exclusion and resource management.

testcases.title: Sv Mailbox
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates SystemVerilog mailbox mechanisms for inter-process communication, covering bounded/unbounded mailboxes, blocking operations (put/get), non-blocking variants (try_put/try_get), peek for non-destructive reads, and parameterized mailboxes with custom transaction classes. Shows practical producer-consumer patterns using fork-join concurrency.

testcases.title: Buggy Ipc Exercise1
testcases.scenario: Multi-producer multi-consumer IPC system using events, semaphores, and mailboxes for synchronization. The design demonstrates concurrent task coordination and shared resource access patterns, but contains critical bugs in semaphore initialization, state tracking, and incomplete code that prevent correct operation.

testcases.title: Buggy Ipc Exercise2
testcases.scenario: Multi-channel arbiter using parameterized mailboxes and semaphores for mutual exclusion, where intentional bugs prevent proper request processing and response delivery. The design demonstrates inter-process communication patterns but contains logic errors in the request handling flow.

testcases.title: Buggy Sv Events Ex1
testcases.scenario: SystemVerilog events exercise where a producer triggers data_ready events while a consumer waits on them. The consumer uses a forever loop with @(data_ready) to process incoming data, but the producer only generates 4 events (i=1 to 4) while the testbench expects 5 receptions, causing a mismatch.

testcases.title: Buggy Sv Events Ex2
testcases.scenario: SV Events exercise demonstrating inter-process communication where a producer triggers data_ready events and a consumer should count and process them. The consumer task contains a bug that prevents proper event handling and data counting.

testcases.title: Buggy Nonblocking Events Ex1
testcases.scenario: Exercise demonstrates nonblocking event triggering (->> operator) in SystemVerilog classes. The buggy code contains a typo in the event trigger statement that prevents proper nonblocking event semantics, causing data value mismatches and incorrect test assertions.

testcases.title: Buggy Nonblocking Events Ex2
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates nonblocking event triggering in SystemVerilog, where a task triggers an event with `->>` (nonblocking) syntax and another task waits for it. The bug involves incorrect expectations about timing and data value propagation when nonblocking events are used.

testcases.title: Buggy Wait Order In Sv Events Ex1
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates the SystemVerilog wait_order() construct for verifying that events occur in a specific sequence. The test attempts to validate that events step1, step2, step3, and step4 fire in the correct order, but there is a critical bug preventing proper sequence verification.

testcases.title: Buggy Wait Order In Sv Events Ex2
testcases.scenario: Exercise demonstrating SystemVerilog wait_order() construct for verifying event ordering constraints. The testbench fires events in both correct and incorrect sequences to verify that wait_order() properly detects ordering violations.

testcases.title: Buggy Merging Events In Sv Ex1
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates event merging in SystemVerilog, where two events can be merged so that triggering one triggers the other. The buggy code attempts to merge evt_b into evt_a but fails to properly synchronize both waiters, resulting in incomplete event propagation.

testcases.title: Buggy Merging Events In Sv Ex2
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates event merging and event reclamation in SystemVerilog, where multiple tasks wait on events and an event is reassigned to a different handle. The bug prevents the merged event from triggering both waiters, causing incomplete event synchronization.

testcases.title: Buggy Passing An Event Ex1
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates passing SystemVerilog events between classes to enable inter-process communication. A Sender triggers events that a Receiver should catch, but the receiver misses events due to a task synchronization issue where the receiver task doesn't start before the sender sends all events.

testcases.title: Buggy Passing An Event Ex2
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates event passing between classes in SystemVerilog, where a Sender triggers events and a Receiver waits on them. The design has a critical loop boundary error that causes the sender to emit one fewer event than intended, resulting in a deadlock where the receiver waits indefinitely for the third event.

testcases.title: Buggy Sv Semaphores Ex1
testcases.scenario: SystemVerilog semaphore exercise demonstrating mutex-protected critical sections and resource pool management. The testbench spawns concurrent tasks that access shared resources, expecting mutex serialization of counter updates and pool-based resource allocation with try_get timeout semantics.

testcases.title: Buggy Sv Semaphores Ex2
testcases.scenario: SystemVerilog semaphore exercise demonstrating mutual exclusion and resource pool management. The design uses a mutex semaphore for critical section protection and a pool semaphore with capacity 3 for resource access, testing blocking get(), non-blocking try_get(), and put() operations.

testcases.title: Buggy Sv Mailbox Ex1
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates SystemVerilog mailbox usage for inter-process communication with producer-consumer patterns and bounded mailbox operations. The bug involves incorrect mailbox behavior in the peek_demo task where get() removes data but the subsequent num() count doesn't match expected behavior.

testcases.title: Buggy Sv Mailbox Ex2
testcases.scenario: SystemVerilog mailbox exercise demonstrating producer-consumer communication with peek and bounded mailbox operations. The design contains a logic error in the consumer task loop that causes incorrect iteration behavior.

testcases.title: Verification Process And Testbench
testcases.scenario: Comprehensive testbench architecture demonstrating industry-standard verification methodology including layered testbench design, transaction-level modeling, and self-checking components. This example covers the complete verification process from test stimulus generation through scoreboarding and functional coverage collection.

testcases.title: Buggy Verification Process And Testbench Exercise1
testcases.scenario: Layered testbench for a round-robin arbiter with incomplete driver implementation and missing interface connections. This exercise demonstrates proper testbench architecture, component connectivity, and the importance of completing all layers before simulation.

testcases.title: Buggy Verification Process And Testbench Exercise2
testcases.scenario: Self-checking testbench for a memory controller that demonstrates basic verification methodology. Contains bugs in transaction generation, assertion placement, and reset sequencing that would cause incorrect verification results or simulation failures.

testcases.title: Immediate Assertions
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates immediate assertions in SystemVerilog including simple assertions, assertions with action blocks (pass/fail), and assumes/covers. Shows how assertions execute immediately in procedural blocks for runtime verification of design behavior.

testcases.title: Boolean Layer
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates the Boolean layer in SystemVerilog assertions, the foundational level of SVA where Boolean expressions evaluate to true/false. Shows how simple signals and logical operators form the basis of concurrent assertion properties that monitor protocol compliance.

testcases.title: Hash Operator
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates the ## (hash) delay operator in SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) for specifying exact clock cycle delays between sequential events. The module illustrates how to write sequences and properties that enforce timing relationships, such as requiring a grant signal exactly 2 cycles after a request.

testcases.title: Dollar Operator
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates SystemVerilog assertion operators ($rose, $fell, $stable, $past) for detecting signal transitions and temporal relationships. These dollar operators are essential for property-based verification, enabling assertions that specify when signals must transition and what values they should hold relative to past cycles.

testcases.title: Repetition Operators
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates SystemVerilog Assertion (SVA) repetition operators including consecutive [*n], range [*n:m], goto [->n], and non-consecutive [=n] repetitions for specifying temporal patterns in protocol sequences and burst transactions.

testcases.title: System Tasks
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates SystemVerilog assertion system tasks including $sampled, $rose, $fell, $stable, $changed, $past, and $countones for temporal property verification. The module implements an interface with data, control, and status signals, and the testbench validates edge detection and sampling behavior across multiple test scenarios.

testcases.title: Binary Operators
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates binary sequence operators (and, or, intersect) in SystemVerilog Assertions for combining and matching multiple sequences. The and operator requires both sequences to complete (possibly at different times), while intersect requires them to match with identical lengths.

testcases.title: Match Operators
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates SystemVerilog Assertion match operators (throughout and within) for checking conditions that must hold during entire sequences or within bounded time windows. The throughout operator ensures expressions remain true for a sequence duration, while within verifies one sequence completes within another's timeframe.

testcases.title: Clocks In Sequence
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates how to specify different clock domains in SystemVerilog assertions using @(posedge clk), @(negedge clk), and default clocking blocks. This module shows clock synchronization across multiple clock domains (main, fast 2x, slow 0.5x) with proper SVA assertions for each domain.

testcases.title: Sequence Arguments
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates parameterized sequences with formal arguments in SystemVerilog assertions, enabling reusable sequence definitions that can be applied to multiple signals and interfaces. Shows how sequence arguments allow flexible property specifications without code duplication across similar protocol patterns.

testcases.title: Local Variables
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates how local variables in SystemVerilog assertions capture values at specific points in time and use them for comparison across subsequent clock cycles. Shows practical applications like data stability checking during handshakes and value tracking across protocol sequences.

testcases.title: Calling Subroutine
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates calling SystemVerilog tasks and functions from SVA sequences using matched sequence endpoints, enabling logging, coverage updates, and side effects when specific protocol patterns occur. This technique bridges assertion verification with dynamic testbench behavior.

testcases.title: A Sequence
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates using SystemVerilog sequences within property definitions for FIFO control verification. Properties wrap sequences with temporal operators to enable assertions, assumptions, and coverage on complex behavioral patterns.

testcases.title: Another Named Property
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates named property declarations in SystemVerilog assertions for an AXI-Lite slave interface, enabling reusable temporal behavior specifications across write and read transactions with proper handshaking.

testcases.title: Negation
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates the 'not' operator in SystemVerilog assertions by implementing a priority arbiter with negation properties to verify that grants are mutually exclusive and that the arbiter correctly handles state transitions. The design shows how negated properties can enforce negative constraints—verifying what should NOT happen rather than what should.

testcases.title: Disjunction
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates the disjunction (or) operator in SystemVerilog assertions to specify alternative valid behaviors. A cache controller uses assertions to verify that transactions result in either cache hits or cache misses, showing how the 'or' operator creates flexible property specifications for complex state machines.

testcases.title: Conjunction
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates SystemVerilog assertion conjunction (and) operator for verifying that multiple properties must hold simultaneously in a DMA controller design. The conjunction requires both source and destination interfaces to be active and valid at the same time, enforcing strict timing constraints between parallel subsystems.

testcases.title: If Else
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates conditional property behavior in SystemVerilog assertions using if-else constructs to specify different verification rules based on transaction type (Memory Read, Memory Write, Completion). This enables flexible assertion specifications where different TLP (Transaction Layer Packet) operations in a PCIe protocol checker follow distinct verification paths.

testcases.title: Implication
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates SystemVerilog implication operators (|-> and |=>) through an I2C master controller with assertions verifying state transitions and protocol compliance. The testbench validates overlapping and non-overlapping implications for protocol sequencing.

testcases.title: Disable Iff
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates the use of 'disable iff' clause in SystemVerilog assertions to handle reset conditions and disable signals. The UART controller example shows how assertions can be safely suspended during reset states and special modes without triggering false failures.

testcases.title: Property Arguments
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates parameterized SVA properties that accept arguments (signals, values, sequences) to create reusable assertion templates for verifying multi-channel memory arbiter behavior. Shows how property arguments enable flexible, configurable assertions that can be instantiated with different signal bindings.

testcases.title: Recursive Property
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates recursive property definitions in SystemVerilog assertions for verifying variable-length packet sequences. A packet processor module uses a state machine to receive, buffer, process, and output packets while assertions monitor the temporal relationships between start-of-packet, payload data, and end-of-packet signals across multiple cycles.

testcases.title: Multi Clock Sequence
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates multi-clock domain crossing using two-stage synchronizers and sequences that span different clock domains. The design safely transfers requests and data from one clock domain to another using proper synchronization techniques and SystemVerilog assertions across clock boundaries.

testcases.title: Multi Clock Property
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates an asynchronous FIFO implementation with multi-clock domain properties using Gray code synchronization. This design validates property assertions that span across independent write and read clock domains with different frequencies (100 MHz vs 80 MHz).

testcases.title: Assert Assume And Cover
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates the three fundamental SystemVerilog assertion constructs (assert, assume, cover) within an SPI master controller design. Shows how assertions verify critical design behaviors, assumptions document input constraints, and cover statements ensure functional coverage.

testcases.title: Binding
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates the bind construct in SystemVerilog for non-invasively attaching assertions to a design module. This lab shows how verification assertions can be cleanly separated from design code, enabling assertion reuse and third-party IP verification without modifying original sources.

testcases.title: Expect
testcases.scenario: This golden reference demonstrates the 'expect' statement in SystemVerilog, a procedural assertion that blocks execution until a property passes or fails and returns a value indicating success. The example shows a Wishbone master controller with a standalone testbench that uses 'expect' statements to verify request-acknowledge handshakes and valid data sequences in procedural code.

testcases.title: Clock Resolution
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates clock resolution rules in multi-clock domains using SystemVerilog assertions. Shows how explicit clock specifications in properties take precedence, and illustrates proper clock synchronization across 100MHz, 200MHz, and 50MHz clock domains with independent request-acknowledge handshakes.

testcases.title: Buggy Systemverilog Assertions Exercise1
testcases.scenario: FIFO protocol assertion exercise with three bugs: wrong clock edge triggering property evaluation, missing next-cycle implication operator, and inverted reset logic in disable condition. Students must identify and fix assertion syntax and semantics errors that prevent proper protocol verification.

testcases.title: Buggy Systemverilog Assertions Exercise2
testcases.scenario: SystemVerilog concurrent assertions module for handshake protocol verification with valid/ready signals. The exercise contains three bugs: incomplete property declaration (missing closing), incorrect sequence syntax for valid hold timing, and incorrect disable condition reset logic.

testcases.title: Buggy Immediate Assertions Ex1
testcases.scenario: A buggy FIFO queue with immediate assertions that demonstrates three assertion mistakes: using assert in always_comb (triggering on X values at time 0), inverting the assertion condition to check the wrong behavior, and using $fatal without proper severity level in the else clause.

testcases.title: Buggy Immediate Assertions Ex2
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates a handshake protocol bug where data latches on (valid || ready) instead of (valid && ready), allowing incorrect transfers when only one signal is asserted. The immediate assertion masks the bug by checking the same incorrect condition, failing to catch the single-signal latch scenario.

testcases.title: Buggy Boolean Layer Ex1
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates three common boolean expression errors in SystemVerilog assertions: using bitwise operators (&, ~) instead of logical operators (&&, !), and incorrect value checks in property conditions. The buggy design attempts to verify request-grant handshaking and data validation but fails due to operator misuse and incorrect assertions.

testcases.title: Buggy Boolean Layer Ex2
testcases.scenario: SystemVerilog testbench for a handshake controller that uses a boolean layer in SVA assertions. The DUT should pulse 'done' for one cycle when both 'valid' AND 'ready' are high simultaneously, but contains a logic error using OR instead of AND.

testcases.title: Buggy Hash Operator Ex1
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates three common mistakes with SystemVerilog delay operators in assertions: using ##0 (same-cycle) instead of ##1 (next-cycle) for sequential checks, specifying range delays with inverted bounds ##[4:1], and incorrectly using ##0 to AND signals in the same cycle. Students must identify and correct these temporal logic errors.

testcases.title: Buggy Hash Operator Ex2
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates incorrect usage of SystemVerilog delay operators (##) in assertions. The design contains three distinct bugs: using ##[0:0] instead of ##[1:1] for next-cycle checks, expecting done at the wrong cycle count (##5 instead of ##4), and chaining ##0 operators which creates a same-cycle AND instead of sequential delays.

testcases.title: Buggy Dollar Operator Ex1
testcases.scenario: SystemVerilog assertion exercise demonstrating three common dollar operator ($) pitfalls: using $rose() on multi-bit signals (only checks LSB), $past() without disable iff triggering during reset, and mutually-exclusive conditions ($rose && $fell in same cycle). Students must identify and fix these assertion bugs to properly monitor handshake and control signals.

testcases.title: Buggy Dollar Operator Ex2
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates SystemVerilog assertion properties using dollar operators for temporal logic. The design implements a simple state machine with start/done handshaking and attempts to verify request stability, data history, and command encoding using SVA properties.

testcases.title: Buggy Repetition Operators Ex1
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates three common mistakes with SystemVerilog assertion repetition operators: using [*0] which matches zero occurrences vacuously, employing [->N] goto with incorrect repetition counts for protocol verification, and using [=N] non-consecutive repetition with wrong multiplicity expectations.

testcases.title: Buggy Repetition Operators Ex2
testcases.scenario: SystemVerilog assertion exercise demonstrating three critical bugs with repetition operators: misuse of zero-or-more [*] causing vacuous matches, incorrect operator precedence binding [*] to wrong operand, and protocol misunderstanding where req[*3] expects 3 consecutive cycles but protocol only holds 1 cycle.

testcases.title: Buggy System Tasks Ex1
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates three common bugs in SystemVerilog system tasks: inverted logic in $isunknown() that incorrectly asserts data must be unknown when valid, use of $onehot() instead of $onehot0() failing when cmd equals zero, and an impossible condition $countones(data) > 8 for 8-bit data where the maximum population count is 8.

testcases.title: Buggy System Tasks Ex2
testcases.scenario: SystemVerilog module with assertion system tasks that violate protocol requirements. The design uses $onehot0() which incorrectly allows zero bits, $stable() as an overly permissive antecedent, and makes incorrect assumptions about data monotonicity in assertions.

testcases.title: Buggy Binary Operators Ex1
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates three binary operator misuses in SystemVerilog assertions: using 'and' between sequences of different length ranges, attempting 'intersect' on non-matching length sequences, and confusing the sequence 'and' operator with boolean AND operations. The testbench verifies proper handshaking and control flow timing.

testcases.title: Buggy Binary Operators Ex2
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates three binary operator bugs in SVA: 'intersect' between sequences with mismatched lengths (2 vs 1 cycle), contradictory sequence definitions that cannot both be true, and missing parentheses for operator precedence in logical combinations.

testcases.title: Buggy Match Operators Ex1
testcases.scenario: This exercise contains three bugs in SystemVerilog assertion match operators: `throughout` incorrectly applied to a property instead of a sequence, `within` operator with swapped operands where the longer sequence should contain the shorter, and `intersect` used with sequences of mismatched lengths that cannot properly align.

testcases.title: Buggy Match Operators Ex2
testcases.scenario: A SystemVerilog design using assertions to verify that a counter-based DUT asserts 'done' exactly 2 clock cycles after 'start' pulses. The bug is a counter threshold mismatch: the DUT uses threshold 3'd3 instead of 3'd2, causing 'done' to assert one cycle too late and fail the ##2 match operator check.

testcases.title: Buggy Clocks In Sequence Ex1
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates multiple clock specification errors in SystemVerilog assertions, including mixing clock domains within a sequence, specifying clock events on wrong signals, and property-sequence clock mismatches. Students must identify and fix incorrect @(clock) syntax and ensure proper clock specification in assertion constructs.

testcases.title: Buggy Clocks In Sequence Ex2
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates three critical clock specification errors in SystemVerilog assertions: using a sequence with its own clock specification inside a property that also specifies a clock, attempting to use ##0 (zero cycle delay) between different clock domains which is illegal, and mismatching the clock edges between sequence and property definitions.

testcases.title: Buggy Sequence Arguments Ex1
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates three critical bugs in SystemVerilog sequence formal argument usage: a type mismatch where an int argument is used as a signal in a sequence expression, an attempt to use a sequence argument directly as a delay value (which requires a constant or parameter), and incorrect sequence instantiation arguments that cause elaboration failures.

testcases.title: Buggy Sequence Arguments Ex2
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates three critical bugs in SystemVerilog sequence argument handling: incorrect default value syntax (`:=` instead of `=`), a sequence local variable that shadows a module port, and improper mixing of positional and named arguments in sequence instantiation. Students must identify and fix these violations of SVA argument semantics.

testcases.title: Buggy Local Variables Ex1
testcases.scenario: SystemVerilog assertion exercise demonstrating three critical bugs with local variables in sequences: uninitialized local variable usage, type mismatch between local variable and assigned signal, and illegal out-of-scope reference to a sequence-local variable in a property.

testcases.title: Buggy Local Variables Ex2
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates three common mistakes with local variables in SystemVerilog assertions: using identical variable names in nested sequences causing scope conflicts, assigning a local variable after it is used in the same expression, and incorrectly declaring local variables in property context instead of sequence context.

testcases.title: Buggy Calling Subroutine Ex1
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates a SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) bug where a function with side effects (modifying req_count) is illegally called within an SVA assertion action block. According to IEEE 1800-2012 §16.8.2, functions called in SVA action blocks must be side-effect-free; the spurious counter increment corrupts the protocol verification logic and masks true assertion failures.

testcases.title: Buggy Calling Subroutine Ex2
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates three critical bugs in SystemVerilog assertion subroutine calling: improper $display syntax in action blocks, attempting to use a void function's return value in a sequence, and incorrectly calling a subroutine in the antecedent instead of the consequent of an implication property.

testcases.title: Buggy A Sequence Ex1
testcases.scenario: SystemVerilog assertions exercise demonstrating three common bugs in sequence and property definition: using sequences without proper reset control, referencing non-existent signals in assertions, and mismatched temporal relationships between property predicates and actual DUT behavior.

testcases.title: Buggy A Sequence Ex2
testcases.scenario: 2-stage pipeline shift register where the second pipeline stage (pipe2) is removed, causing output to appear 1 cycle early instead of the correct 2-cycle latency. The testbench verifies timing by checking that dout matches din exactly 2 cycles after din is loaded, exposing the missing pipeline stage.

testcases.title: Buggy Another Named Property Ex1
testcases.scenario: SystemVerilog assertions exercise demonstrating three distinct timing and reset logic bugs: req |=> gnt incorrectly expects delayed grant (DUT requires simultaneous), p_gnt_ack checks one-cycle-delayed ack incorrectly, and p_no_disable fires during reset due to missing disable iff. The module implements a handshake protocol where ack is the registered AND of synchronous req and gnt inputs.

testcases.title: Buggy Another Named Property Ex2
testcases.scenario: SystemVerilog assertion exercise demonstrating three common property specification bugs: missing clock specification that relies on implicit inference, combining properties with mismatched timing specifications using 'or', and using an incorrect clock edge (negedge instead of posedge) in an assertion statement.

testcases.title: Buggy Negation Ex1
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates three common negation mistakes in SystemVerilog assertions: applying 'not' to a sequence instead of promoting it to a property first, using double negation which is semantically equivalent to the original property, and incorrectly negating implication properties which reverses their intended behavior.

testcases.title: Buggy Negation Ex2
testcases.scenario: SystemVerilog assertion exercise demonstrating the 'not' operator in SVA properties. The DUT should suppress output when an error signal is asserted, but contains a logic bug where the output combinational logic uses OR instead of AND-NOT, causing the assertion to fail when both err and in are high.

testcases.title: Buggy Disjunction Ex1
testcases.scenario: Two-requester bus arbiter with a buggy disjunction property. The arbiter should grant (gnt=1) one cycle after either req_a OR req_b is asserted, but uses AND (req_a & req_b) instead of OR, causing gnt to remain low when only one requester is active.

testcases.title: Buggy Disjunction Ex2
testcases.scenario: A SystemVerilog module with a multiplexer bug where the output always computes x+1 regardless of the mode_a signal. The SVA property uses disjunction to specify that either mode_a selects (x+1) or the inverted path (~x), but the missing conditional assignment prevents the second branch from ever executing.

testcases.title: Buggy Conjunction Ex1
testcases.scenario: A dual-channel memory design with write and read logic where a logic error prevents channel B from being updated. The testbench performs simultaneous writes to both channels and verifies that data can be read back correctly, exposing the missing write path for channel B.

testcases.title: Buggy Conjunction Ex2
testcases.scenario: SystemVerilog assertion exercise testing conjunction of two sequence requirements in a handshake protocol. The DUT incorrectly drives ack based only on req, ignoring the gnt signal, causing ack to assert even when gnt is low—violating the second branch of the conjunction property that requires ack to remain low when gnt is absent.

testcases.title: Buggy If Else Ex1
testcases.scenario: SystemVerilog assertion exercise with three intentional bugs: an assignment operator (=) used instead of comparison (==) in the if condition, incorrect delay specification (##2 instead of ##1) for mode 01, and wrong signal checked (ack instead of gnt) in the else branch.

testcases.title: Buggy If Else Ex2
testcases.scenario: SystemVerilog SVA property with inverted if-else condition that mismatches the DUT pipeline latency. The property expects a 1-cycle response when cmd==2'b01, but the DUT implements a 2-cycle slow path for all non-zero cmd values, causing assertion failures.

testcases.title: Buggy Implication Ex1
testcases.scenario: SystemVerilog assertion exercise demonstrating three critical implication timing bugs: using overlapping (|->) instead of non-overlapping (|=>) operators, operator-DUT timing mismatches, and incorrect property antecedents that reverse the logical dependency.

testcases.title: Buggy Implication Ex2
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates a non-overlapping implication (|=>) bug where a request-grant arbiter uses a two-stage pipeline register instead of one, causing the grant signal to appear two cycles after a request instead of the required one cycle. Students must identify and fix the extra pipeline delay to satisfy the SVA property req |=> gnt.

testcases.title: Buggy Disable Iff Ex1
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates three common mistakes with SystemVerilog assertion disable_iff clauses: using active-low reset polarity incorrectly (rst_n instead of !rst_n), attempting to place disable_iff in the wrong syntactic position, and using overly complex disable conditions that mask legitimate assertion violations. Students must identify and correct these disable_iff usage errors to properly gate assertions during reset and other disable conditions.

testcases.title: Buggy Disable Iff Ex2
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates three common mistakes with SystemVerilog assertion disable_iff clauses: using non-standard equality comparison (==) instead of logical negation, disabling assertions based on data values that should actually be checked, and using multi-bit signals directly in disable conditions without proper boolean conversion. Students must identify and correct these disable_iff usage patterns.

testcases.title: Buggy Property Arguments Ex1
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates parameterized SVA property reuse across multiple channels; Channel 1 has a hardwired grant signal (gnt_ch1 <= 1'b0) instead of following the request, causing the req |=> gnt assertion to fail.

testcases.title: Buggy Property Arguments Ex2
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates three common mistakes when using parameterized properties and sequences in SystemVerilog assertions: incorrect default parameter values, improper named argument syntax, and passing complex expressions where simple signals are expected. Students must identify and fix syntax errors and semantic bugs in property declarations and instantiations.

testcases.title: Buggy Recursive Property Ex1
testcases.scenario: A SystemVerilog counter module with a bounded-liveness SVA property that documents the countdown behavior. The DUT decrements by 2 instead of 1, causing odd load values to skip zero and wrap around, violating the property that done must assert within 16 cycles of start.

testcases.title: Buggy Recursive Property Ex2
testcases.scenario: SystemVerilog assertion exercise demonstrating bugs in recursive property definitions and their interaction with reset logic and signal inversions. The design attempts to implement a request-grant-acknowledge protocol but contains multiple flaws: inverted ACK generation, recursive properties without proper disable conditions, and mismatched consequents between related assertions.

testcases.title: Buggy Multi Clock Sequence Ex1
testcases.scenario: Two-clock-domain CDC (Clock Domain Crossing) design where a fast-clock input is synchronized to a slow clock using a synchronizer. The design should employ a 2-stage flip-flop synchronizer to safely cross clock domains, but only one synchronization stage is implemented, causing the output to appear one slow-clock cycle too early.

testcases.title: Buggy Multi Clock Sequence Ex2
testcases.scenario: Multi-clock sequence design where an event from clock domain A must be captured and synchronized into clock domain B within 2 clk_b cycles. The bug causes the capture register to use clk_a instead of clk_b, making captured_b update on the wrong clock edge and presenting stale data when sampled at clk_b posedge.

testcases.title: Buggy Multi Clock Property Ex1
testcases.scenario: A simplified CDC FIFO with two pipeline stages crossing clock domains from clk1 to clk2. Stage 1 captures input data (din) into stage1_reg when wr_en is asserted in the clk1 domain, and Stage 2 re-registers stage1_reg into dout in the clk2 domain. The design demonstrates multi-clock property verification and data synchronization across asynchronous clock domains.

testcases.title: Buggy Multi Clock Property Ex2
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates three common multi-clock property specification bugs: combining properties across different clock domains using 'and', using 'or' between incompatible clocking contexts, and omitting explicit clock specifications in properties that require them. The design attempts to verify request-grant-acknowledge handshaking across multiple clock domains, but the assertions are incorrectly structured.

testcases.title: Buggy Assert Assume And Cover Ex1
testcases.scenario: SystemVerilog module with three assertion-related bugs: using assume instead of assert for property checking, incorrectly adding an else action block to a cover property, and confusing the context of assert property statements. The module implements a simple request-grant-acknowledge handshake with flawed formal properties.

testcases.title: Buggy Assert Assume And Cover Ex2
testcases.scenario: SystemVerilog FSM with assertion properties that checks state transitions. The design should transition from IDLE → ACTIVE → DONE on start and finish pulses, but a duplicate state encoding prevents the FSM from reaching the DONE state, causing assertions to fail.

testcases.title: Buggy Binding Ex1
testcases.scenario: A counter module with a synchronous reset that incorrectly loads 8'hFF instead of 8'h00, which is caught by an SVA assertion bound to the DUT without modifying the original source code. The exercise demonstrates how bind statements attach checkers to verify DUT behavior independently.

testcases.title: Buggy Binding Ex2
testcases.scenario: SystemVerilog binding exercise demonstrating three critical assertion bugs: incorrect port mapping in bind statement (req/gnt swapped), assertion property checking wrong timing relationship (same-cycle implication instead of sequential), and multiple conflicting bind instances creating redundant or contradictory checks.

testcases.title: Buggy Expect Ex1
testcases.scenario: A sequential state machine counts exactly 4 clock cycles after start assertion, then pulses done for one cycle. The testbench uses SVA expect to verify done arrives at the correct cycle.

testcases.title: Buggy Expect Ex2
testcases.scenario: A SystemVerilog testbench using `expect` statements to verify a two-stage handshake protocol: req → gnt (within 1 cycle) → ack (within 1 cycle). The DUT contains an extra pipeline register that delays ack by 2 cycles instead of 1, causing the second expect statement to fail.

testcases.title: Buggy Clock Resolution Ex1
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates clock domain conflicts in SystemVerilog assertions where a default clocking block is defined but properties and sequences specify different clock edges, creating ambiguity and potential assertion failures. The design has three related bugs: redundant clock specification overriding the default clocking, negedge sequence conflicting with posedge property semantics, and mismatched clocking between property declarations and their usage.

testcases.title: Buggy Clock Resolution Ex2
testcases.scenario: SystemVerilog assertion exercise with multiple clock resolution bugs: a default clocking block using negedge when the DUT transitions on posedge, causing sampling mismatches between assertions and actual design behavior. The exercise demonstrates why explicit clock specifications in properties are critical and how default clocking edge selection can silently break assertion correctness.

testcases.title: Uvmconfigdb
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates UVM ConfigDB usage for setting and retrieving virtual interfaces and configuration objects across testbench hierarchy. Shows proper configuration propagation patterns, hierarchical scoping, and best practices for managing agent configurations in UVM environments.

testcases.title: Buggy Uvmconfigdb Exercise1
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates three common UVM ConfigDB mistakes: incorrect hierarchical path in set(), type mismatch between set() and get() calls, and attempting to set configuration values after the build_phase when they are already consumed. Students must identify and fix these bugs to properly propagate configuration parameters through the UVM component hierarchy.

testcases.title: Buggy Uvmconfigdb Exercise2
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates UVM ConfigDB usage with virtual interfaces and wildcard scoping. Students must identify three bugs: incorrect null context and path in virtual interface retrieval, missing virtual interface configuration before component build, and mismatched field names in exists() versus get() calls.

testcases.title: Buggy Uvmfactory Exercise1
testcases.scenario: UVM factory override exercise demonstrating how to properly register and override transaction classes. The test creates transaction objects using both direct instantiation and factory methods, then checks if factory overrides correctly produce extended transaction types instead of base types.

testcases.title: Buggy Uvmfactory Exercise2
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates UVM factory pattern with instance overrides and component creation. Students must fix an incorrect instance override path that prevents the fast_drv from being substituted for base_drv, and identify missing factory diagnostics.

testcases.title: Buggy Set Inst Override Ex1
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates UVM factory instance override usage where a base component should be replaced with an override component. The test incorrectly specifies the instance path in set_inst_override_by_type, using 'env.wrong_name' instead of the actual hierarchical path 'env.comp', causing the override to fail silently.

testcases.title: Buggy Set Inst Override Ex2
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates UVM factory set_inst_override_by_type() with a critical bug: the instance override uses an incorrect path 'env.wrong_name' instead of 'env.comp', and the component is created via new() instead of factory create(), preventing the override from taking effect.

testcases.title: Buggy Set Inst Override By Name Ex1
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates UVM factory instance override functionality using set_inst_override_by_name(). The test attempts to override base_comp with override_comp, but uses an incorrect instance path pattern that fails to match the target component during creation.

testcases.title: Buggy Set Inst Override By Name Ex2
testcases.scenario: UVM factory override exercise where set_inst_override_by_name is correctly called to replace base_comp with override_comp, but the override fails to apply because comp is instantiated using direct new() instead of the factory type_id::create() method.

testcases.title: Buggy Set Inst Override By Type Ex1
testcases.scenario: A UVM testbench that attempts to override a component instance type using set_inst_override_by_type, but fails because the instance path string doesn't match the actual hierarchy. The test creates an env with a comp instance but tries to override using 'env.wrong_name' instead of 'env.comp'.

testcases.title: Buggy Set Inst Override By Type Ex2
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates UVMFactory's set_inst_override_by_type() mechanism, where components can be overridden during build phase. The test expects an override_comp instance to be created instead of base_comp, but the override fails due to an incorrect instance path specification in the override call.

testcases.title: Buggy Set Type Override Ex1
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates UVM factory type override mechanism where a derived component (override_comp) should replace a base component (base_comp) in the factory. The bug shows incorrect argument order in set_type_override_by_type(), which reverses the intended override relationship and fails to instantiate the derived class.

testcases.title: Buggy Set Type Override Ex2
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates UVM factory pattern type overrides where a test attempts to override base_comp with override_comp. The bug occurs because the test_env instantiates comp using direct instantiation (new) instead of factory creation (create), causing the type override to be bypassed and the wrong component type to be instantiated.

testcases.title: Buggy Set Type Override By Name Ex1
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates UVM factory type override by name, where a derived class (override_comp) should replace instances of a base class (base_comp). The bug involves swapped argument order in set_type_override_by_name(), causing the wrong type to be registered for override.

testcases.title: Buggy Set Type Override By Name Ex2
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates a UVM factory override mechanism that fails because the component is instantiated using direct new() instead of the factory's type_id::create() method. Even though set_type_override_by_name() is correctly called, the override cannot be applied since the component bypasses the factory.

testcases.title: Buggy Set Type Override By Type Ex1
testcases.scenario: A UVM factory override exercise where set_type_override_by_type() arguments are reversed, causing the factory to override override_comp with base_comp instead of the intended base_comp with override_comp. The test instantiates a base_comp but expects the factory override to substitute an override_comp instance.

testcases.title: Buggy Set Type Override By Type Ex2
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates UVM factory override mechanism using set_type_override_by_type(). The test expects that when base_comp is overridden with override_comp, instantiating base_comp should create override_comp instead. However, override_comp is missing the `uvm_component_utils macro registration, and the env uses direct instantiation (new) instead of factory creation, preventing the override from taking effect.

testcases.title: Inst Override
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates proper use of UVM factory pattern with set_inst_override to dynamically substitute component types at runtime. Shows how factory create() respects type overrides registered in the factory, enabling flexible test configuration without recompilation.

testcases.title: Inst Override By Name
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates UVM factory pattern with set_inst_override_by_name, showing how to create multiple agent instances and override specific instances by hierarchical path. The test creates two APB agents, each with its own driver and sequencer, illustrating component instantiation through the factory and the ability to selectively override component types at runtime.

testcases.title: Inst Override By Type
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates UVM Factory's set_inst_override_by_type mechanism, where type overrides registered during build_phase affect factory creation calls. Shows how apb_agent instances created via type_id::create() honor any active overrides, enabling dynamic component substitution without modifying source code.

testcases.title: Type Override
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates proper use of UVM factory pattern with set_type_override to dynamically substitute component types at runtime. Shows factory-based creation in build_phase, factory configuration queries in end_of_elaboration_phase, and the component topology that results from factory overrides.

testcases.title: Type Override By Name
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates UVM factory pattern with type_id::create() for polymorphic component instantiation. Shows how the factory system enables runtime type overrides and proper component hierarchy establishment through build_phase.

testcases.title: Type Override By Type
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates UVM factory pattern with set_type_override_by_type to substitute derived driver and sequencer types at runtime. Shows how factory-created components respect type overrides established before elaboration, enabling flexible testbench architecture without code modification.

testcases.title: Uvmobjection
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates proper objection management in a UVM testbench hierarchy by showing how structural containers (agent, env) delegate objection responsibility to the test and sequences, while the driver runs passively in a forever loop consuming transactions until the run_phase terminates.

testcases.title: Buggy Uvmobjection Exercise1
testcases.scenario: This exercise demonstrates improper UVM objection handling where drop_objection is called prematurely, terminating the run_phase before component work completes. Students must identify that the test drops its objection after only 200ns while the components require 500ns (5 work items × 100ns each) to finish, causing incomplete execution and phase termination issues.

testcases.title: Buggy Uvmobjection Exercise2
testcases.scenario: This buggy exercise demonstrates a missing raise_objection() call in the run_phase of a UVM component, causing the phase to complete before the component finishes its work. The missing objection allows the simulator to advance past run_phase without waiting for the 100-time-unit delay to complete.

testcases.title: Uvmphases
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates UVM component hierarchy and phase execution ordering, showing how build_phase executes top-down to create components while connect_phase executes bottom-up to establish port connections between driver, monitor, and scoreboard.

testcases.title: Buggy Uvmphases Exercise1
testcases.scenario: UVM testbench with three distinct bugs in phase implementation: build_phase missing super.build_phase() call prevents configuration propagation, connect_phase attempting to access an uninitialized late_comp handle, and run_phase missing objection handling that prevents proper phase termination.

testcases.title: Buggy Uvmphases Exercise2
testcases.scenario: This UVM testbench exercise demonstrates incorrect phase management and objection handling. It contains multiple bugs in phase execution: an objection raised in phase_ready_to_end without a corresponding drop mechanism, attempting to access run-time data (main_count) in an elaboration-time function, and an off-by-one loop iteration in main_phase. These errors violate UVM phase semantics and cause simulation hangs or incorrect counter values.

testcases.title: Uvmreporting
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates UVM reporting mechanisms including field macros (`uvm_field_int`), nested object printing via `do_print()`, and various `uvm_report_*` functions with different verbosity levels and printer types (table, tree, line). Shows how to structure data item classes and leverage UVM's built-in print infrastructure for debugging and verification.

testcases.title: Buggy Uvmreporting Exercise1
testcases.scenario: UVM reporting exercise demonstrating incorrect severity levels, verbosity settings, and report action configurations that suppress or incorrectly classify messages during simulation.

testcases.title: Buggy Uvmreporting Exercise2
testcases.scenario: This UVM reporting exercise demonstrates custom report catching and ID-based filtering. Students must identify three bugs: an unregistered report catcher, an ID verbosity mismatch, and an invalid max_quit_count setting that prevents normal test termination.

testcases.title: Buggy Uvmruntest Exercise1
testcases.scenario: UVM test demonstrating improper test registration and factory instantiation. The exercise exposes how missing `uvm_component_utils` macros prevent factory-based component creation, and how objection handling affects simulation termination.

testcases.title: Buggy Uvmruntest Exercise2
testcases.scenario: Exercise demonstrates UVM objection mechanism in run_phase where missing raise_objection() allows phase to exit before long-running work completes, combined with a timeout value that's too short to accommodate work duration and potential phase completion issues.

testcases.title: Rtl
testcases.scenario: A simple 8-bit counter module that demonstrates basic synchronous design with reset, load, and enable control signals. It showcases fundamental RTL patterns including asynchronous reset, priority-based control logic, and registered output that counts on clock edges.

testcases.title: Tb
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates a complete UVM testbench architecture with agent, driver, and environment components that implement a counter DUT interface using clocking blocks and sequencer-driver handshaking for stimulus generation and response capture.

testcases.title: Tests
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates UVM test hierarchy and phase management with a base test class that handles reset and report phases, extended by concrete test classes that override main_phase to run specific sequences. Shows proper use of objection handling, virtual interfaces, and test result reporting.

testcases.title: Uvmactvpassvagent
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates a single reusable UVM agent class that conditionally creates active (driver + sequencer + monitor) or passive (monitor-only) components based on the is_active configuration. Uses get_is_active() checks during build_phase and connect_phase to tailor component instantiation and connectivity.

testcases.title: Buggy Uvmactvpassvagent Exercise1
testcases.scenario: UVM agent with active/passive mode configuration demonstrating proper driver/monitor instantiation and config_db usage. The design shows how agents conditionally build drivers based on is_active mode while monitors operate in both modes.

testcases.title: Buggy Uvmactvpassvagent Exercise2
testcases.scenario: UVM passive agent with three critical issues: missing super.build_phase() call in monitor preventing proper UVM infrastructure initialization, analysis_port never connected to any subscriber in the passive agent, and incorrect is_active configuration value set via config_db. This exercise tests understanding of passive agent construction, port connectivity, and configuration mechanisms.

testcases.title: Buggy Uvmsequence Exercise1
testcases.scenario: UVM sequence exercise demonstrating sequence item generation and sequencer communication. The design shows write and read sequences that generate bus transactions, but contains critical bugs in sequence execution flow and randomization timing that prevent proper stimulus generation.

testcases.title: Buggy Uvmsequence Exercise2
testcases.scenario: UVM sequence hierarchy exercise demonstrating virtual sequences and sequencer communication. The design shows a virtual sequence that should orchestrate sub-sequences on a target sequencer, but contains critical bugs in sequencer reference management and synchronization lock handling.

testcases.title: Buggy Uvmseqdrvrseqrcommunication Ex1
testcases.scenario: UVM sequence-driver communication exercise demonstrating proper sequence item creation, randomization, and driver handshaking. The code attempts to send randomized sequence items from a sequence through a sequencer to a driver, but contains a critical bug in the sequence body that prevents correct item transmission.

testcases.title: Buggy Uvmseqdrvrseqrcommunication Ex2
testcases.scenario: A UVM testbench where a sequence sends items to a driver through a sequencer, but the driver fails to call item_done() after processing each item, causing the sequence to hang indefinitely waiting for the driver to release the item.

testcases.title: Buggy Uvmsequencelib Ex1
testcases.scenario: This UVM testbench demonstrates a sequence-driver communication pattern but contains multiple critical bugs preventing proper item flow between the sequencer and driver. The exercise requires identifying missing connections, incomplete macros, and improper sequence usage.

testcases.title: Buggy Uvmsequencelib Ex2
testcases.scenario: A UVM testbench with a sequence, sequencer, and driver that demonstrates basic stimulus generation and transaction handling. The code is incomplete, with a connection statement cut off mid-line in the connect_phase.

testcases.title: Buggy Uvmsequencemacros Ex1
testcases.scenario: UVM sequence exercise demonstrating improper use of sequence macros and sequence item generation. The code attempts to create and randomize sequence items but contains critical errors that prevent proper sequence execution and driver-sequencer communication.

testcases.title: Buggy Uvmsequencemacros Ex2
testcases.scenario: UVM testbench with a sequence, driver, and environment that fails to properly connect the driver's sequence item port to the sequencer. The test class definition is incomplete and the environment's connect_phase does not establish the required port connection.

testcases.title: Buggy Uvmsequencemethods Ex1
testcases.scenario: UVM sequence fails to properly generate and send sequence items to the driver. The sequence creates an item but never uses `start_item()`/`finish_item()` protocol, and the body task is missing a loop to generate multiple items, causing the driver to hang waiting for items.

testcases.title: Buggy Uvmsequencemethods Ex2
testcases.scenario: UVM sequence that attempts to send randomized items through a sequencer-driver connection. The sequence uses start_item/finish_item but has a critical syntax error that prevents compilation.

testcases.title: Buggy Uvmsequencerarbitration Ex1
testcases.scenario: UVM testbench demonstrating sequence-to-driver communication via sequencer arbitration. The test creates a driver and sequencer but fails to establish the critical port connection and complete the test class definition, preventing proper item flow.

testcases.title: Buggy Uvmsequencerarbitration Ex2
testcases.scenario: A UVM testbench with a sequence, driver, and sequencer demonstrating sequence-driver arbitration. The design attempts to execute a simple sequence that generates random transaction items and sends them through the sequencer to the driver for processing.

testcases.title: Buggy Uvmsequencerlockandgrab Ex1
testcases.scenario: UVM sequence exercise demonstrating sequencer lock/grab mechanism where a sequence attempts to communicate with a driver. The design contains a critical bug in the sequence body that prevents proper item generation and sequencer interaction.

testcases.title: Buggy Uvmsequencerlockandgrab Ex2
testcases.scenario: UVM testbench with a sequencer and driver that fails to connect, and an incomplete test class definition that cannot compile. The sequencer never delivers items to the driver due to the missing port connection in connect_phase.

testcases.title: Buggy Uvmsequencestart Ex1
testcases.scenario: A UVM testbench that demonstrates sequence-driver interaction, where a sequence generates randomized transaction items and a driver consumes them. The test should send multiple transactions through the sequencer to the driver.

testcases.title: Buggy Uvmsequencestart Ex2
testcases.scenario: A UVM testbench demonstrating sequence and driver interaction where the base_env connect_phase contains an incomplete port connection statement. The design attempts to create a simple transaction sequence but fails due to a truncated connection line that prevents proper sequencer-driver communication.

testcases.title: Buggy Uvmvirtualsequence Ex1
testcases.scenario: UVM testbench demonstrating a virtual sequence integration bug where the sequencer is not connected to the driver, preventing proper communication between sequence and driver components.

testcases.title: Buggy Uvmvirtualsequence Ex2
testcases.scenario: A UVM testbench where a sequence sends transaction items through a sequencer to a driver, but the driver fails to call item_done() after processing each item, causing the sequence to hang indefinitely waiting for the driver to release the transaction.

testcases.title: Uvmseqdrvrseqrcommunication
testcases.scenario: This golden reference demonstrates two primary UVM driver-sequencer communication patterns: Approach A using get_next_item()/item_done() for synchronized blocking communication, and Approach B using get()/put() for decoupled request-response handling. The example shows how TLM port connections enable different synchronization semantics between sequence execution and driver activity.

testcases.title: Uvmsequencelib
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates UVM sequence library patterns including base sequence inheritance, constraint-driven randomization, and runtime sequence registration via add_sequence(). Shows proper use of sequencer item flow (start_item/finish_item) with inline randomization and helper methods for transaction printing.

testcases.title: Uvmsequencemacros
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates a complete UVM agent hierarchy with driver and sequencer connected via sequence item ports, showing how sequence macros enable communication between sequences and drivers in a testbench environment.

testcases.title: Uvmsequencemethods
testcases.scenario: Demonstrates UVM agent architecture with driver-sequencer connection and response handling. The driver processes sequence items, simulates memory operations (read/write), and returns responses via item_done(), illustrating proper seq_item_port communication patterns and response generation for sequence-driver interaction.

testcases.title: Uvmsequencestart
